title: Oral liquid volumes from mg/5 mL and mg/1 mL
blurb: Calculate the volume of an oral liquid from its label strength, including the stock volume, and give it to the decimal places asked.
question: A person is prescribed morphine sulfate 2.5 mg. The oral solution is labelled 10 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given?

teach.h: Want over have, times the volume
teach.body: Formal rule: volume = (dose wanted ÷ dose in stock) × stock volume. Plain English: the label tells you how many mg are in a set volume (often 5 mL). Find what fraction of that amount you need, then take that fraction of the volume. Every Part A paper has an oral liquid item read from a bottle label.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 4 (liquid dose); Pearson VUE NMC practice papers

head: Label
mg in 1 mL
Stock volume to use
teach.caption: Either use the label as written with its volume, or convert to mg per 1 mL first: both give the same answer.

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Fletcher at home
teach.body: Joan Fletcher, 79, is visited by the district nurse. She is prescribed morphine sulfate 2.5 mg; the oral solution is 10 mg/5 mL. Volume = 2.5 ÷ 10 × 5 = 0.25 × 5 = 1.25 mL. Sense-check: 2.5 mg is a quarter of 10 mg, so a quarter of 5 mL. If asked for two decimal places, type 1.25 mL.

teach.text: Forgetting to multiply by the stock volume: treating "10 mg/5 mL" as if it were 10 mg in 1 mL. The answer comes out five times too small.

items.label: if the dose is less than the mg in 5 mL
if the dose is more than the mg in 5 mL

teach.h: What volume is on the label?

teach.body: Keep every digit on the calculator until the final volume, then round to the instruction: "one decimal place" or "two decimal places". Rounding the fraction first (for example 0.248 to 0.25) shifts the answer. Volumes are typed with the unit: 7.5 mL, not 7.50 mL and not 7.5 mls.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice tests, answer-format guidance

items: mg/5 mL means multiply by 5; mg/mL means multiply by 1.
Classic error: forgetting the stock volume (answer five times too small).
Round only the final answer, to the stated decimal places.
Type the number and mL, with no trailing zeros.

summary: You can now calculate oral liquid volumes from mg/5 mL and mg/mL labels using want ÷ have × volume. You can also round once at the end and type the volume in Pearson's format.

A.q: A person is prescribed 400 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Used 50 mg (the mg per mL) as if it were the mg per 5 mL.

A.q: A service user is prescribed amitriptyline 30 mg. The oral solution is labelled 25 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Gave the label volume, which holds 25 mg, not 30 mg.

A.q: A client is prescribed levetiracetam 750 mg. The oral solution is labelled 100 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: The label is per 1 mL. Volume = 750 ÷ 100 × 1 = 7.5 mL.

whyNot.1: Multiplied by 5 as if the label were per 5 mL.
whyNot.3: Misread 100 mg as 10 mg, a tenfold error.

B.q: A child is prescribed paracetamol 180 mg. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Used 100 mg/5 mL, not the 120 mg/5 mL on the label.

B.q: A person is prescribed morphine sulfate 7.5 mg. The oral solution is labelled 10 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

B.q: A child is prescribed cefalexin 125 mg. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Read the label as 125 mg/5 mL, half its real strength: 5 mL of this suspension holds 250 mg, double the dose.

C.q: A client is prescribed carbamazepine 300 mg twice a day. The oral liquid is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What total volume is given in 24 hours? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: One dose = 300 ÷ 100 × 5 = 15 mL. Twice a day: 15 × 2 = 30 mL.

whyNot.0: This is one dose, not the 24-hour total.

C.q: A person is prescribed phenytoin 100 mg. The oral suspension is labelled 30 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
C.why: Volume = 100 ÷ 30 × 5 = 16.666… mL, which is 16.67 mL to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

C.q: A client is prescribed sodium valproate 340 mg. The oral solution is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Rounded 1.7 to 2 before multiplying: rounding too early.

reteach.title: Don't forget the 5 mL
reteach.question: The label says 125 mg/5 mL and you need 125 mg. What volume is that?

blocks.body: "125 mg/5 mL" means 125 mg is dissolved in every 5 mL. Needing 125 mg means 5 mL. Needing 250 mg means 10 mL. The volume always travels with the mg.

blocks.text: 125 ÷ 125 = 1 is the fraction of the 5 mL, not the volume. Multiply by 5.

explain.body: Want (prescription), have (mg on the label) and volume (mL on the label). Volume = want ÷ have × volume.

test.q: A child is prescribed 150 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Used 250 mg/5 mL, double the strength on the label.

test.q: A person is prescribed 25 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 10 mg/1 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Multiplied by 5 as if the label were per 5 mL.

test.q: A person is prescribed 35 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 50 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

explain.body: 62 ÷ 250 = 0.248. Keep it: 0.248 × 5 = 1.24. Rounding 0.248 to 0.25 first gives 1.25, which is marked wrong.

test.q: A child is prescribed 62 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Rounded 0.248 to 0.25 before multiplying: rounding too early.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
